# Forge

> Forge is an internet-native programming language implemented in Rust. HTTP client and server, SQLite/Postgres/MySQL, JSON, CSV, crypto, JWT, regex, filesystem, shell, and concurrency are built in, with no imports or packages. Source files use the `.fg` extension.

This file is the canonical, compact guide for AI models writing Forge. Every code block below was run on Forge v0.9.x with the default engine (`forge run file.fg`). Prefer the forms shown here.

Write only the forms shown here. Edition 2026 (the default) also accepts an older "natural" syntax (`set x to 5`, `say`, `define`, `otherwise`, `repeat n times`, `unpack`, `must`, `safe`, `check`, ...) and joke builtins (`sus`, `bruh`, ...); edition 2027 (`forge --edition 2027`, or `edition = "2027"` under `[project]` in forge.toml) removes them, and `forge fix --edition 2027` rewrites old code.

## Running

```
forge run app.fg                 # run (bytecode VM, the default engine)
forge --interp run app.fg        # tree-walking interpreter (reference semantics)
forge --jit run app.fg           # VM + Cranelift JIT for numeric functions
forge --allow-run run app.fg     # allow sh/run_command and other shell builtins
forge -e 'println(1 + 2)'        # evaluate inline
forge --edition 2027 run app.fg  # edition 2027 (preview); `forge fix --edition 2027 .` migrates 2026 code
forge test                       # run @test functions in tests/*.fg
forge build --native app.fg      # native executable (also: fmt, new, lsp, add, install)
forge mcp --allow-net=api.x.com  # MCP server: AI agents run Forge in a deny-all sandbox (VM; --engine interp)
forge mcp serve tools.fg         # serve @tool functions as MCP tools
forge run --max-fuel 1000000 --max-memory 64MB f.fg  # deterministic step budget + memory cap ("fuel exhausted" / "memory limit exceeded", not catchable)
```

Engine flags go BEFORE the subcommand: `forge --interp run x.fg`, not `forge run x.fg --interp`. Operators: `+ - * / %`, `== != < <= > >=`, `&& || !`, `+=`.

## Reading input

Programs read piped standard input with `fs.lines("/dev/stdin")` (an array of lines, without the newlines) or `fs.read("/dev/stdin")` (all of it as one string). `input()` also returns all of stdin, with trailing whitespace trimmed. Command-line arguments: `forge run main.fg --top 3 data.txt` passes everything after the file name to the program (flags included; forge's own flags go before the file). `io.args()` is the script path followed by those arguments (`["main.fg", "--top", "3", "data.txt"]`), so the arguments are `slice(io.args(), 1, len(io.args()))`. `io.args_get("--top")` is the value after a flag (`"3"`, a String; `true` for a flag followed by another flag or nothing; `null` if absent), `io.args_has("--verbose")` tests a flag, `io.args_parse()` returns `{"--top": "3", ...}`; all three ignore the arguments after a `--`. Under `--sandbox` the program still gets its arguments.

```forge
let lines = fs.lines("/dev/stdin")
let mut total = 0
for line in lines {
    if trim(line) != "" {
        total += int(trim(line))
    }
}
println("lines={len(lines)} total={total}")
```

## Values, variables, strings

```forge
let name = "Forge"            // immutable binding
let mut count = 0             // mutable binding
count += 1
count = count + 1
let pi = 3.14                 // Float
let ok = true                 // Bool
let nothing = null            // Null
let nums = [1, 2, 3]          // Array
let user = { name: "Ada", age: 36 }   // Object (string keys, insertion-ordered)
let pair = (1, "one")         // Tuple
println("Hello, {name}! count={count}")   // "{expr}" interpolates inside double-quoted strings
println("{join(["a", "b"], ", ")}")       // any expression, including string literals: a, b
println(typeof(pi))           // Float
println(user.name)
println(nums[0])
println(nums[-1])             // 3: negative indexes count from the end
println(len(nums))
println(str(42) + "!")        // + joins two Strings; convert other values with str() or "{x}"
println(int("7") + 1)
println(10 / 4)               // 2 (Int / Int is integer division)
println([1, 2] + [3])         // [1, 2, 3] (+ also joins two arrays)
println(abs(-3))              // 3
println(min(4, 2), max([4, 9]))   // min/max take numbers or one array
println(round(3.14159, 2))    // 3.14 (round(x) alone gives an Int: 3)
println(to_fixed(2.5, 2))     // 2.50 (a String with exactly 2 decimals)
let {name: who, age} = user     // destructuring (also `let [first, ...rest] = nums`, `let (a, b) = pair`)
let [first, ...rest] = nums
println("{who} {age} {first} {rest}")
```

Numbers: literals are `42`, `1_000_000` (underscores ignored), `3.14`, and with an exponent `1e9`, `2.5e-3`, `6E+23` (an exponent always makes a Float: `1e2` is `100.0`). A whole Float prints without decimals (`println(3.0)` prints `3`), so format money and averages with `to_fixed(x, digits)` (also `x.to_fixed(2)`, `"{to_fixed(x, 2)}"`); it rounds half away from zero on the exact value. `round(x)` returns an Int, `round(x, digits)` a Float. `abs`, `min`, `max`, `round`, `floor` and `ceil` keep Ints as Ints (`floor`/`ceil` of a Float is an Int).

Types: `Int`, `Float`, `String`, `Bool`, `Null`, `Array`, `Object`, `Tuple`, plus `Set`, `Map`, `Result`, `Option`, structs and algebraic types. `typeof(x)` returns one of `Int`, `Float`, `String`, `Bool`, `Null`, `Array`, `Object` (also for struct and algebraic values), `Tuple`, `Set`, `Map`, `Result`, `Option`, `Function` (a named `fn`), `Lambda` (an anonymous `fn`), `BuiltIn`, `Channel`. Strings cannot be indexed (`s[0]` is an error): use `substring(s, start, end)`. Annotations are optional: `let t: Int = 42`, `fn f(x: Int) -> String`. Comments are `//`. Escapes in `"..."` strings: `\n` `\t` `\r` `\\` `\"`, `\{` and `\}` (a literal brace, never an interpolation), and Unicode escapes `\u{e9}` / `\u{1F600}` (1 to 6 hex digits) or `\u00e9` (exactly 4; a surrogate pair `\uD83D\uDE00` is one character); anything else (`\0`, `\x41`) is a syntax error. `chr(n)` is the one-character string for code point `n` (`chr(233) == "é"`), `ord(s)` the code point of a one-character string (`ord("A") == 65`). Triple-quoted `"""..."""` strings span lines and are raw: no escapes, no interpolation (use them for regexes with `{`). In `"..."` strings, digit-only braces such as `\\d{4}` or `{2,}` and Unicode classes such as `\\p{L}` are literal.

## Type annotations and checking

Annotation syntax: `Int`, `[Int]`, `?String` (or `Option<String>`), `Result<Int, String>`, `Object` (any object), `Object<Int>` (an object whose values are all Int: a typed dictionary, e.g. `let ages: Object<Int> = { ada: 36 }` or a parsed JSON object), `Map<String, Int>` (a `Map` value from `map()`; an object literal is not a Map), `Set<Int>`, `(Int, String)`, `fn(Int, Int) -> Bool`, `Any`, user structs/types, generics `fn first<T>(xs: [T]) -> T`, `struct Box<T> { value: T }`.

```forge
fn apply(f: fn(Int) -> Int, x: Int) -> Int { return f(x) }
let twice: fn(Int) -> Int = fn(n) { n * 2 }   // n inferred as Int
let names = ["ada", "bob"]
let lens = map(names, fn(s) { len(s) })        // lens: [Int]
```

Every program is type-checked before it runs (gradual: unannotated code is inferred, unknown things are `Any`). Diagnostics have stable codes: T0001 type mismatch, T0002 argument type, T0003 return type, T0004 argument count, T0005 invalid operator (`"a" - 1`), T0006 unknown name (with did-you-mean), T0007 unknown struct field, T0008 unknown module member (`math.sqr`), T0009 missing return, T0010 unreachable code, T0011 non-exhaustive match, T0012 interface not satisfied, T0013 not callable, T0014 Option used as its value, T0015 unknown type, T0016 missing struct field, T0017 assignment to immutable `let`, T0018 used before definition, T0019 discarded `push(xs, v)` result (edition 2027), T0020 import not found (the message shows the path it looked for), T0021 an import renames a struct/type/variant/interface (`import { Point as P }`). Edition 2026 (default): warnings, the program still runs. `forge run --strict file.fg`: diagnostics are errors, and annotated function arguments/results are also checked at run time (`type error: argument 'n' of 'double' must be Int, got String`).

Edition 2027 (`edition = "2027"` in forge.toml, or `forge --edition 2027`): annotations are enforced. A contradiction of a declared type (T0001, T0002, T0003, T0012, T0015, T0016) or an import that cannot be found or renames a type (T0020, T0021) is an error and nothing runs; annotated function arguments and results are checked at run time on every call (E0017); unannotated code is not checked and costs nothing. Generic parameters must agree within a call: `fn pair<T>(a: T, b: T)` accepts `pair(1, 2)` and `pair(1, 2.5)` (T is Float) but not `pair(1, "x")`. So annotate function signatures with the types you mean (`fn total(xs: [Int]) -> Int`), and leave unknowns unannotated rather than guessing. A declared `Float` (parameter, return type, annotated `let`, struct field) turns an Int into a Float in 2027 and under `--strict`: `fn half(x: Float) -> Float { return x / 2 }` gives `half(3) == 1.5`, `let y: Float = 7` is `7.0`. Edition 2026 without `--strict` never converts (`half(3)` is `1`): write `float(x)` there when a value may be an Int.

## Control flow

```forge
let score = 85
if score >= 90 {
    println("A")
} else if score >= 80 {
    println("B")
} else {
    println("C")
}

for i in range(0, 3) {        // 0, 1, 2 (end is exclusive); also: for x in array
    println(i)
}
for e in enumerate(["x", "y"]) {   // enumerate yields { index, value }
    println("{e.index}: {e.value}")
}
for k, v in { a: 1, b: 2 } {       // two-variable form is for objects and maps
    println("{k}={v}")
}

let mut n = 0
while n < 3 {
    n += 1
}

let mut m = 0
loop {
    m += 1
    if m == 2 { continue }
    if m >= 4 { break }
}
println(score > 0 && score < 100)
let grade = if score >= 50 { "pass" } else if score >= 30 { "retry" } else { "fail" }   // `if` is an expression (with `else if`); there is no `cond ? a : b`
println(grade)
```

## Functions and closures

```forge
fn add(a, b) {
    return a + b
}

fn greet(name: String) -> String {
    return "Hello, {name}!"
}

let square = fn(x) { return x * x }   // anonymous function

fn make_counter() {
    let mut count = 0
    return fn() {
        count += 1
        return count
    }
}

println(add(2, 3))
println(greet("Ada"))
println(square(4))
let c = make_counter()
c()
println(c())                  // 2
```

Always write an explicit `return`.

Top-level `fn` definitions are hoisted: `let avg = mean(nums)` may come before `fn mean(xs) { ... }` in the file (also in imported modules and test files). A function that reads a top-level variable becomes callable once that variable is defined. A name defined twice (or a builtin's name) is not hoisted.

## Structs, methods, interfaces

```forge
struct Point {
    x: Int,
    y: Int
}

impl Point {
    fn sum(it) {              // `it` is the receiver (like self)
        return it.x + it.y
    }
}

let p = Point { x: 1, y: 2 }
println(p.sum())

struct User {
    name: String,
    role: String = "member"   // field default
}
let u = User { name: "Ada" }

interface Describable {
    fn describe() -> String
}

impl Describable for User {
    fn describe(it) {
        return it.name + " (" + it.role + ")"
    }
}
println(u.describe())
println(satisfies(u, Describable))
```

Values are copied (structs, arrays, objects), and a method's receiver `it` is
read-only. A method that updates its receiver declares it `mut it`; when it
returns, the updated `it` is written back to the variable (or field/index of
one) the method was called on:

```forge
struct Stack {
    items: [Int]
}

impl Stack {
    fn push(mut it, x: Int) {      // `mut it`: updates the receiver
        it.items.push(x)
    }
    fn pop(mut it) {
        return it.items.pop()
    }
    fn peek(it) {                  // plain `it`: read-only
        return it.items[len(it.items) - 1]
    }
}

let mut s = Stack { items: [] }    // the receiver must be `let mut`
s.push(1)
s.push(2)
println(s.pop())                   // 2
println(s.items)                   // [1]
let mut stacks = { a: Stack { items: [] } }
stacks.a.push(7)                   // fields and elements update in place too
```

- Assigning to a plain `it` (`it.n += 1`, `it.items.push(x)`, `it = ...`) is
  an error (E0006 / T0017); copy it first (`let mut c = it`) to return a
  modified value instead.
- A `mut it` method on a `let` (immutable) binding is E0006; on a temporary
  (`make().inc()`, `a.b().inc()`) it is E0006 "cannot update a temporary
  value". Works the same for `type` (algebraic) methods and through interfaces.
- The update is written back only when the method returns normally; an error
  inside it leaves the receiver unchanged.

A parameter declared with an interface (`fn show(d: Describable)`) accepts any struct that has the interface's methods, and passes on to another parameter of that interface, or of an interface whose methods it has (`fn report(d: Describable) { show(d) }`).

## Algebraic types and match

```forge
type Shape = Circle(Float) | Rect(Float, Float)

impl Shape {
    fn area(it) {
        match it {
            Circle(r) => { return 3.14159 * r * r }
            Rect(w, h) => { return w * h }
        }
    }
}

for s in [Circle(1.0), Rect(2.0, 3.0)] {
    println(s.area())
}

match Rect(2.0, 5.0) {
    Circle(r) => println("circle {r}"),
    Rect(w, h) => println("rect {w}x{h}"),
}

let v = 7
match v {
    0 => println("zero"),
    7 => println("seven"),
    _ => println("other"),
}
```

`match` is also an expression: its value is the taken arm's value (an arm body is an expression or a `{ ... }` block whose last expression is the value), so it works in `let`, `return`, arguments and lambdas.

```forge
fn size(n) {
    return match n {
        0 => "none",
        1 | 2 => "few",                  // or-pattern
        x if x < 10 => "some {x}",       // guard: a false guard tries the next arm
        _ => "many",
    }
}
println(size(2))
println(size(7))

type Shape = Circle(Float) | Rect(Float, Float) | Square(Float, Float)
let s = Square(2.0, 2.0)
let label = match s {
    Circle(r) if r > 10.0 => "big circle",
    Circle(r) => "circle {r}",
    Rect(w, h) | Square(w, h) => {
        let area = w * h
        "box of area {area}"
    },
}
println(label)
```

Patterns: literals (including negative numbers), `_`, bindings, constructors `Name(a, b)` (nested: `Ok(Some(x))`), and or-patterns `p1 | p2` whose alternatives bind the same names. There are no array or tuple patterns (`[a, b] =>` and `(a, b) =>` are syntax errors): destructure first (`let [a, b] = pair`) or nest matches. A guard `pattern if cond` sees the pattern's bindings. If no arm matches, it is a runtime error (E0026); end with `_ => ...` when the cases are open.

## Result, Option, errors

```forge
fn parse_age(s) {
    let n = int(s)
    if n < 0 {
        return Err("negative age")
    }
    return Ok(n)
}

fn next_age(s) {
    let n = parse_age(s)?          // ? returns the Err early, unwraps the Ok
    return Ok(n + 1)
}

let good = next_age("41")
if is_ok(good) {
    println("ok {unwrap(good)}")
}
let bad = next_age("-3")
println(is_err(bad))
println(unwrap_or(bad, 0))

let found = Some(3)
println(is_some(found))
println(is_none(None))
match found {
    Some(x) => println("got {x}"),
    None => println("none"),
}

try {
    let z = 1 / 0
} catch e {
    println("caught {e.type}: {e.message}")   // ArithmeticError: division by zero
}
try {
    unwrap(Err("bad config"))    // unwrap: the value, or raise the error
} catch e {
    println(e.message)
}
```

The type checker narrows an optional value after a null test: in `if x != null { ... }`, after `if x == null { return ... }`, and on the right of `x != null && x > 0` / `x == null || v < x`, `x` is not null (no T0014 warning).

There is no `throw`. Return `Err(...)` and propagate with `?`, or raise with `assert(cond, msg)` / `unwrap(expr)` (both are catchable). `?` only works on `Result` values; `?` at the top level of a program stops it with `unhandled error: ...`. To ignore a block's errors, use `try { ... } catch e { }`.

Error codes: every runtime error has a stable code, the same on both engines; type-checker diagnostics are `T0001`–`T0021`. `forge explain E0009` prints an explanation, example and fix; `forge explain` lists all codes. A caught error `e` has `e.message` (without the hint), `e.code`, `e.hint` (the error's suggestion, or `null`) and `e.type`, a category that is the same for every error of a code (shown in the table). Branch on `e.code`, not on message text. The runtime codes:

| code | `e.type` | raised by |
|---|---|---|
| `E0000` | RuntimeError | anything without a more specific code (e.g. `toml.parse` of bad text) |
| `E0003` | ReferenceError | undefined name |
| `E0004` / `E0005` | TypeError | calling a non-function / wrong argument count |
| `E0006` | TypeError | assigning to an immutable binding |
| `E0007` | TypeError | operator on unsupported types (`[1] * 2`) |
| `E0008` | ArithmeticError | division or modulo by zero |
| `E0009` | IndexError | index out of bounds (`xs[5]`) |
| `E0010` | ReferenceError | missing key (`m["nope"]`) |
| `E0011` | TypeError | value cannot be indexed that way (`null["x"]`, `5[0]`, `"abc"[0]`: use `substring`) |
| `E0012` / `E0014` | TypeError | field access on `null` / on a non-object |
| `E0013` | ReferenceError | unknown field or method |
| `E0015` | TypeError | bad builtin argument (`len(5)`, `join([1], 5)`) |
| `E0016` | RuntimeError | stdlib operation failed (`fs.read` of a missing file, a failed command) |
| `E0017` | TypeError | value does not match its annotation (edition 2027, `--strict`) |
| `E0019` / `E0020` | ReferenceError / RuntimeError | import failed / permission denied |
| `E0021` | AssertionError | `assert`, `assert_eq`, ... failed |
| `E0023` / `E0024` | RuntimeError | `unwrap` of `None`/`Err` / `?` on an `Err` at the top level |
| `E0026` | RuntimeError | no `match` arm matched |
| `E0030` | RuntimeError | `send` on a closed channel |
| `E0031` | TimeoutError | `timeout` block expired, `--max-time`, cancelled |
| `E0034` | TypeError | edition 2027: `"a" + 1` |
| `E0036` / `E0037` | TimeoutError / ConnectionError | HTTP request timed out / could not connect |
| `E0038` | ValueError | `int("12x")`, `float("abc")`: text is not a number |
| `E0039` | ValueError | invalid JSON (`json.parse`, `fs.read_json`, `sh_json`) |
| `E0040` | ValueError | invalid regex pattern |
| `E0041` | RuntimeError | `retry n times` exhausted (the message ends with the last attempt's error) |

For tools: `forge check file.fg` type-checks without running, and `--error-format json` (or `forge check --format json`) prints one `{code, severity, message, file, line, col, hint, phase}` object per diagnostic.

```forge
try {
    let xs = [1, 2, 3]
    println(xs[5])
} catch e {
    println(e.code)          // E0009
}
```

## Modules

```forge
import { double, shout } from "utils.fg"   // selected names
println(double(21))
import { name as user_name } from "lib/user.fg"   // renamed: binds user_name
import { sqrt, pi } from "math"            // members of a built-in module
println(sqrt(16))                          // math.* stays available too
import "lib/geo.fg" as geo                 // namespace: geo.<name>
println(geo.area(geo.Circle(2.0)))         // functions, variables, variants
let p = geo.Point { x: 1, y: 2 }           // structs: geo.Point { ... }, geo.Point.origin()
match shape { geo.Circle(r) => r, geo.Dot => 0.0 }   // variants in patterns
```

A module exports every name its top level binds: functions, `let` variables (destructured ones too), structs, interfaces, `type` names and their variants, and the names it imports itself (re-exports: a package's `main.fg` can `import { parse } from "src/parser.fg"` and its users `import { parse } from "pkg"`). Import a type with its variants, `import { Shape, Circle, Dot } from "shapes.fg"`, to write `fn area(s: Shape)` (the type name alone does not bring its variants; as a value it is its description, `Shape.variants == ["Circle", "Dot"]`). Interfaces import the same way: `import { Plugin } from "api.fg"` then `impl Plugin for Upper { ... }`.

`import "m.fg" as m` binds `m` to a read-only namespace object: its members are the module's exports (plus `m.__module__`, the path). It is the same module run as every other import of the file (shared state); a variable member is the value when the import ran, like `import { x }` — read changing state through a function. `m.nope` is error E0013 `module 'm.fg' has no member 'nope'` with a did-you-mean (T0008 statically, and `m.f(x)` is checked against `f`'s signature); `m.x = 1` is the immutable-assignment error. `m` can be passed around (`typeof(m)` is `Object`). Built-in modules cannot be renamed (`import "math" as m` is E0019).

`as` renames functions and variables (use it when two modules export the same name); a struct, `type`, variant or interface keeps its own name (renaming one is an import error). A module runs once per program: importing it again — from another module, or with `import "m.fg"` after `import { f } from "m.fg"` — reuses it, so its top-level code runs once and every importer shares its state (`let mut` counters, caches). This holds across `spawn` tasks too: a module first imported inside a task is not run again when the program or another task imports it (a task importing a module another task is still running waits for it). But a task works on a copy of the program's state, so what a task writes to a module's variables is not seen outside it: return results with `await` or channels. Import cycles are an error (`circular import: a.fg -> b.fg -> a.fg`).

Native plugins (Rust/C shared libraries built with `crates/forge-plugin`): `import native "target/release/libfoo" as foo` then `foo.add(1, 2)`, or `import { add } from native "path/libfoo"`. The platform suffix is added; paths resolve like `.fg` imports. Needs `--allow-ffi` (full trust; denied under `--sandbox` and `forge mcp`). Plugin errors are catchable runtime errors.

`import "utils.fg"` brings every top-level definition into scope (not the names `utils.fg` itself imports). A path resolves relative to the importing file first, then the current working directory, then the installed packages (`forge_modules/<name>/main.fg`, `forge_modules/<name>.fg`, `forge_modules/<name>/src/main.fg`); the `.fg` suffix is optional. Stdlib modules (`math`, `fs`, `http`, ...) are always in scope; never import them. Packages are declared in `forge.toml` (`forge add <pkg>`).

## Collections and builtins

```forge
let nums = [5, 3, 8, 1]
let mut xs = [1, 2]
xs = push(xs, 3)              // push returns a new array: reassign it
xs.push(4)                    // or append in place (method form)
let top = pop(xs)             // pop(xs) / xs.pop() remove and return the last element
let mut groups = { a: [] }
groups["a"].push(1)           // the method form also updates a field/index place
groups.a.push(2)              // (the root must be `let mut`); groups is { a: [1, 2] }
println(map(nums, fn(x) { return x * 2 }))
println(filter(nums, fn(x) { return x > 2 }))
println(reduce(nums, 0, fn(acc, x) { return acc + x }))   // (array, initial, fn)
println(sort(nums))
println(sort(nums, fn(a, b) { return b - a }))            // comparator returns a number
println(nums.filter(fn(x) { return x % 2 == 1 }).map(fn(x) { return x * 10 }))
println(find(nums, fn(x) { return x > 4 }))
println(contains(nums, 8))

let mut user = { name: "Ada", age: 36 }
user.email = "ada@example.com"
println(keys(user))
println(get(user, "missing", "default"))
println(pick(user, ["name"]))
println(merge(user, { age: 37 }))

let s = "Hello, World"
println(split(s, ", "))
println(join(["a", "b"], "-"))
println(replace(s, "World", "Forge"))
println(s.upper())
println("  pad  ".trim())
println(starts_with(s, "Hell"))
println(substring(s, 0, 5))
println(contains(s, "lo, W"))

let st = set([1, 2, 2, 3])
println(st.has(2))
let mut m = map()
m = m.set("k", 1)             // set/remove return a new Map: reassign
println(m.get("k"))
println([1, 2, 3, 4].stream().filter(fn(x) { return x > 1 }).take(2).collect())
```

Maps: `m.set(k, v)` and `m.remove(k)` return a new Map (a bare `m.set(k, v)` statement changes nothing), `m.get(k)` (`null` if absent), `m.has(k)`, `m.keys()`, `m.values()`, `m.len()`, `m.to_array()` (an array of `(key, value)` tuples), `for k, v in m`; `m[k]` is an error. Keys may be any value (`1` and `1.0` are one key, NaN finds NaN, arrays/objects/sets compare by content); for String keys an object (`obj[k] = v`) is simpler. Maps and sets are hash-indexed: `get`/`has`/`set`/`remove` (and set `has`/`add`/`remove`) take constant time on average, and `m = m.set(k, v)` / `m = m.remove(k)` on a `let mut` variable update it without copying the map, so building a map in a loop is linear.

Other builtins: `exit(code)` (ends the program at once with that exit status; output already printed is kept), `eprintln(...)` / `eprint(...)` (like `println`/`print`, to stderr: warnings and errors of CLI programs), `abs(x)`, `min(a, b, ...)` / `min(array)`, `max`, `round(x, digits?)`, `floor(x)`, `ceil(x)`, `to_fixed(x, digits)`, `len`, `range`, `reverse`, `sum`, `any`, `all`, `unique`, `zip(a, b)`, `chunk(arr, n)`, `slice(arr, start, end)`, `has_key`, `flatten`, `min_of`, `max_of`, `values`, `omit`, `entries`, `ends_with`, `index_of`, `slugify`, `chr(n)`, `ord(s)`, `uuid()`, `typeof`, `str`, `int`, `float`, `wait(seconds)` (fractions allowed: `wait(0.25)`), `assert`, `assert_eq`.

## Standard library (always in scope)

| Module | Most-used functions (argument order matters) |
| ------ | -------------------------------------------- |
| `math` | `sqrt(x)`, `pow(b, e)`, `abs`, `max(a, b)`, `min`, `floor`, `ceil`, `round`, `random_int(lo, hi)`, `pi`, `e` |
| `fs` | `read(path)`, `write(path, text)`, `append`, `exists`, `list(dir)`, `remove`, `mkdir`, `copy(src, dst)`, `rename` |
| `json` | `parse(text)` (keeps the document's key order), `stringify(value)` → `{"a": 1, "b": [1, 2]}`, `compact(value)` → `{"a":1,"b":[1,2]}` (no whitespace), `pretty(value, indent?)`; numbers keep their kind: integer syntax parses as Int (`-0` is `0`; beyond 64 bits a Float), `1.0`/`1e2` as Float, and a Float is written with a fraction (`json.compact(1.0)` is `1.0`, NaN/infinity `null`); strings use `\b \f \n \r \t \" \\` and `\u00XX` |
| `regex` | `test(text, pattern)`, `find(text, pattern)` (first match or `null`), `find_all(text, pattern)`, `captures(text, pattern)` (first match's groups `[whole, g1, g2, ...]`, an unmatched group `null`; `null` when nothing matches), `captures_all(text, pattern)` (one such array per match), `replace(text, pattern, repl)` (`repl` may use `$1`, `$0`, `$$`, and `${name}` for `(?<name>...)` in a `"""..."""` string), `split(text, pattern)` — text FIRST |
| `crypto` | `sha256(s)`, `md5(s)`, `base64_encode`, `base64_decode`, `hex_encode`, `hex_decode` |
| `http` | `get(url, opts?)`, `post(url, opts?)`, `put`, `delete`, `patch`, `head`; opts: `{ body, headers, params, timeout, auth }` (a String `body` is sent as is, any other value as JSON; `timeout` is in seconds, default 30, `0.5` allowed); response: `{ status, ok, body, json, headers }` (`body` is the text, `json` the parsed body); a 4xx/5xx answer is a normal response with `ok == false`; no answer raises `E0036` (timed out) or `E0037` (refused, unknown host, TLS) |
| `db` | SQLite: `open(path)`, `execute(sql, params?)`, `query(sql, params?)` → array of objects, `last_insert_rowid()`, `begin()`/`commit()`/`rollback()`, `close()` |
| `pg`, `mysql` | `connect(url)`, `query(conn, sql, params?)`, `execute(conn, sql, params?)`, `close(conn)`; mysql adds `begin/commit/rollback` |
| `jwt` | `sign(claims, secret, opts?)`, `verify(token, secret)`, `decode(token)`, `valid(token, secret)` |
| `csv` | `parse(text, opts?)` (RFC 4180: quoted fields keep commas, quotes and line breaks; rows are objects keyed by the header; unquoted fields that are exactly an integer, a decimal or `true`/`false` become numbers/booleans, anything else (`02134`, `+1`, `1e5`, quoted text) stays a String; `opts`: `{ header: false }` gives arrays, `{ types: false }` keeps every field a String), `stringify(rows)`, `read(path, opts?)`, `write(path, rows)` |
| `env` | `get(name, default?)`, `set`, `has`, `keys` |
| `log` | `info`, `warn`, `error`, `debug` (structured, via tracing) |
| `term` | `red`, `green`, `bold`, `table(rows)`, `bar`, `sparkline`, `banner`, `box` |
| `time` | `now()` → `{ iso, unix, unix_ms, year, month, day, hour, minute, second, weekday, weekday_short, day_of_year, timezone }` (UTC); `unix()` (Int seconds); `parse(s)` (`2024-03-05`, `2024-03-05 10:20:30`, `2024-03-05T10:20:30Z` or with an offset, converted to UTC) → the same object; `format(t, "%Y-%m-%d")` (`t` an object or Unix seconds, strftime pattern, default `%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S`, always UTC); `add(t, secs)` / `add(t, { days: 1, hours: 2 })`, `sub` → object; `diff(a, b)` (a − b) → `{ seconds, minutes, hours, days, weeks, human }`; `sleep(seconds)` |
| `os`, `path` | `os.platform()`, `os.cpus()`; `path.join(a, b)`, `path.extname(p)`, `path.basename(p)` |
| `io` | `args()` (script path, then the program's arguments), `args_get(flag)`, `args_has(flag)`, `args_parse()`, `prompt` |

`fetch(url)` is shorthand for `http.get`. Shell builtins: `sh(cmd)`, `sh_lines`, `sh_ok`, `sh_json`, `run_command`, `pipe_to(data, cmd)` (need `--allow-run`).

```forge
println(math.sqrt(16.0))
println(regex.find_all("a1b22c333", "\\d+"))
println(regex.replace("a1b2", "\\d", "#"))
let kv = regex.captures("user=ada id=7", "user=(\\w+) id=(\\d+)")   // ["user=ada id=7", "ada", "7"]
println("{kv[1]} {int(kv[2]) + 1}")
println(regex.replace("2024-01-15", "(\\d+)-(\\d+)-(\\d+)", "$3.$2.$1"))   // 15.01.2024
println(json.stringify({ a: [1, 2] }))
println(json.compact({ b: 1, a: [1, 2] }))   // {"b":1,"a":[1,2]}
println(json.parse("[1, 2]")[1])
println(env.get("FORGE_LLMS_UNSET", "fallback"))
println(path.join("a", "b.txt"))
fs.write("/tmp/forge_llms_demo.txt", "line1\nline2")
println(fs.read("/tmp/forge_llms_demo.txt"))
fs.remove("/tmp/forge_llms_demo.txt")
let tok = jwt.sign({ uid: 1 }, "secret")
println(jwt.verify(tok, "secret").uid)
```

## Concurrency

```forge
// Structured concurrency: all spawns join before the block ends; results in spawn order
let results = squad {
    spawn { 1 + 1 }
    spawn { 2 + 2 }
}
println(results)              // [2, 4]

let h = spawn { 40 + 2 }      // detached task
println(await h)
println(await_all([spawn { 1 }, spawn { 2 }]))

let ch = channel()            // unbounded; channel(n) is bounded
spawn {
    send(ch, "ping")
    send(ch, "pong")
}
println(receive(ch))
println(receive(ch))

let t = spawn {
    wait(1)
    return "late"
}
println(await_timeout(t, 10))  // null on timeout (milliseconds)
```

Also: `try_send(ch, v)` (true when sent), `try_receive(ch)` (`Some(v)`, or `None` when nothing is waiting), `close(ch)` (later `send`s fail with E0030; values sent before stay receivable, then `receive` returns `null`), `is_closed(ch)` (true once the channel is closed *and* drained: nothing more can arrive), `select(channels, timeout_ms?)` (`[index, value]` from the first channel with a value; skips finished channels; `null` on timeout, and at once when every channel is closed and drained). After `select` returns `null`, `all(chs, fn(c) { return is_closed(c) })` tells "all producers finished" from "timed out":

```forge
let a = channel()
spawn {
    send(a, 1)
    close(a)
}
let mut got = []
while true {
    let r = select([a], 1000)
    if r == null {
        if is_closed(a) {
            break       // finished, not slow
        }
        continue
    }
    got.push(r[1])
}
println(got)   // [1]
```

A program ends when its top level ends: detached `spawn` tasks still running are abandoned (`await` them to wait).

Tasks communicate through return values (`squad` results, `await`) and channels. Do not mutate captured variables from inside `spawn` and expect the parent to see it: the default VM gives each task its own copy (the `--interp` engine shares closure state).

## Retry, timeout, schedule

Three statement blocks (all editions). They are statements, not expressions: `let r = retry 3 times { ... }` does not parse. To get a value out, assign to a `let mut` declared before the block, or `return` from inside it in a function (a `return`, `break` or `continue` inside the block leaves it at once, without retrying).

```forge
let mut calls = 0
fn flaky() {
    calls += 1
    if calls < 3 {
        let empty = []
        return empty[0]     // fails twice: index out of bounds
    }
    return "ok on attempt {calls}"
}

fn fetch_with_retry() {
    retry 5 times {
        return flaky()      // the first attempt that does not fail returns
    }
}
println(fetch_with_retry())    // ok on attempt 3

try {
    retry 2 times {
        assert(false, "still down")
    }
} catch e {
    println("{e.code}: {e.message}")   // E0041: retry failed after 2 attempts: assertion failed: still down
}

try {
    timeout 1 seconds {
        wait(3)
    }
} catch e {
    println("{e.code}: {e.message}")   // E0031: timeout: operation exceeded 1 second limit
}
```

- `retry n times { body }` runs `body` until it finishes without an error, at most `n` times, waiting 100 ms, 200 ms, ... between attempts. Any runtime error is retried (resource limits are not). When every attempt fails it raises E0041 `retry failed after n attempts: <the last error>`. `n` is an Int (0 or less: the block never runs and the error is raised at once).
- `timeout n seconds { body }` stops `body` (including waits, `receive`, loops and calls inside it) after `n` whole seconds and raises E0031 `timeout: operation exceeded n second limit`; catch it with `try`/`catch`.
- `schedule every n seconds { body }` (or `minutes`, `hours`) runs `body` repeatedly in the background, first after one interval, while the rest of the program continues; it stops when the program ends (a script's top level returns, or never for an HTTP server). It works on its own copy of the program's variables (kept from one run to the next, never seen by the rest of the program), so report results through a channel, a file or a database, not by assigning variables. An error in one run is ignored; the next run still happens. In an `@server` program schedules start after the top level, next to the server.

```forge
let ticks = channel()
schedule every 1 seconds {
    send(ticks, "tick")
}
println(receive(ticks))   // after about a second: tick
```

## HTTP server

```forge
@server(port: 8080)

@get("/hello/:name")
fn hello(name: String) -> Json {
    return { greeting: "Hello, {name}!" }
}

@get("/search")
fn search(query) -> Json {
    return { q: query.q }
}

@post("/echo")
fn echo(body: Json) -> Json {
    return { received: body }
}

db.open("app.db")                      // opened once; every handler uses it
db.execute("CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS items (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT)")

@post("/items")
fn create(body, req) {
    if typeof(body) != "Object" || !has_key(body, "name") {
        return http.response(400, { error: "name is required" })
    }
    let token = get(req.headers, "authorization")   // lower-case names; null if absent
    if token != "Bearer secret" {
        return http.response(401, { error: "unauthorized" }, { "WWW-Authenticate": "Bearer" })
    }
    db.execute("INSERT INTO items (name) VALUES (?)", [body.name])
    let id = db.last_insert_rowid()
    return http.response(201, { id: id, name: body.name }, { Location: "/items/{id}" })
}

@get("/items/:id")
fn show(id) {
    let rows = db.query("SELECT id, name FROM items WHERE id = ?", [int(id)])
    if len(rows) == 0 {
        return http.response(404, { error: "no item {id}" })
    }
    return rows[0]
}

@delete("/items/:id")
fn remove(id) {
    db.execute("DELETE FROM items WHERE id = ?", [int(id)])
    return http.response(204)              // no body
}
```

Handler parameters bind by name: path params (`:name`), `body`/`data` (the request body, `{}` when there is none), `query`/`qs` (all query params), `headers` (request headers, lower-case names), `raw_body` (the body's exact text before decoding, `""` when there is none: use it to check webhook signatures), `req`/`request` (the whole request: `method`, `path`, `params`, `query`, `headers`, `body` — `null` when there is none — and `raw_body`), or a single query param by its name. Path, query and header values are Strings; read an optional one with `get(obj, key)` (indexing a missing key is an error).

Request bodies are decoded by `Content-Type`: JSON (`application/json`, `*+json`) is parsed, a form (`application/x-www-form-urlencoded`) becomes an object of Strings, anything else (text, or no content type) is a String. Invalid JSON is answered `400 {"error": "invalid JSON body: ..."}` and a body that is not UTF-8 text `415` (whatever the content type), before the handler runs.

Returning a value answers `200` with it as JSON. `http.response(status, body?, headers?)` chooses the response: `status` is an Int from 200 to 599; a `null` body sends no body (`204`, redirects), a String is sent as is (`text/plain; charset=utf-8` unless a `Content-Type` header is given), anything else as JSON. Header values are Strings (numbers and Bools are converted; an array sends the header once per value, e.g. `Set-Cookie`); a value with a line break, an invalid name or `Content-Length` is a runtime error. A handler error (or `must Err(...)`) answers `500 {"error": message}`.

Decorators: `@server(port:, host:, cors:)`, `@get`, `@post`, `@put`, `@patch`, `@delete`, `@ws`. The server binds `127.0.0.1` by default with same-origin CORS (`cors: "permissive"` to open it). Each request runs in an isolated fork, so handler mutations of top-level variables do not persist across requests. A database the top level opens (`db.open`, `pg.connect`) is shared by every handler (and by `spawn`ed tasks): statements of concurrent requests run one at a time, a transaction (`db.begin()` ... `db.commit()`) is private to the request that opened it and is rolled back if the request ends without committing, and `db.last_insert_rowid()` is the request's own last insert. `db.open` inside a handler opens a connection for that request only. Server programs run on the bytecode VM by default (`forge --interp run` serves on the interpreter; responses are identical). Unknown decorators or non-literal `@server` arguments make the program fall back to the interpreter automatically.

## Tests

Put `@test fn test_name() { assert_eq(1 + 1, 2) }` functions in `tests/*.fg` and run `forge test` (`forge --allow-run test` if tests use the shell).

## MCP tools (forge mcp serve)

`forge mcp serve tools.fg` serves the file's `@tool` functions to AI agents over the Model Context Protocol. Parameter types become the JSON Schema (`Int` integer, `Float` number, `String`, `Bool`, `[T]` array, `Object` object, `Object<T>` object whose values are `T` (`additionalProperties`), a struct object, `?T`/`Option<T>` or a default make it optional; the arguments arrive as Forge values of those types, so declare a JSON object parameter `Object<T>`, not `Map<String, T>`); the return type becomes the output schema (`Result<T, E>` describes `T`).

```
struct Report { city: String, temp_c: Float }

@tool(description: "Weather for a city (sample data)", read_only: true)
@param(city: "City name")
fn weather(city: String, unit: String = "C") -> Result<Report, String> {
    if city == "Oslo" { return Ok(Report { city: "Oslo", temp_c: -3.0 }) }
    return Err("unknown city: " + city)
}

@resource(uri: "weather://cities", description: "Known cities")
fn cities() { return ["Oslo"] }
```

`@tool` needs a description (`@tool("...")` also works); optional `name`, `title`, `timeout` (seconds), `read_only`, `destructive`, `idempotent`, `open_world`. `@param(name: "doc", ...)` documents parameters. Decorator arguments must be constants. Return `Err(msg)` for a tool error. The top level runs once at start-up; each call runs in a fresh sandboxed fork of it (deny-all plus the server's `--allow-*` grants, `--max-time`), so calls never share state. With plain `forge mcp`, `run_forge` takes an optional `session_id` that keeps top-level variables between calls; `reset_session` clears it. `run_forge` returns what the program printed as `stdout` and what it wrote to stderr (`eprintln`, and `log.info/warn/error/debug` as `[level] message` lines) as `stderr`; both count against one output limit.

## Common mistakes

- Destructure with `let`: `let {a, b} = obj`, `let {a: x} = obj` (renames), `let [x, ...rest] = arr`, `let (a, b) = tuple`; add `mut` for mutable bindings. Missing fields/items bind `null`.
- Words like `order`, `from`, `to`, `limit`, `where`, `select`, `table`, `take`, `times`, `safe` are fine as variable, function, parameter and field names. Reserved: `let mut fn return if else match for in while loop break continue struct type interface impl pub import spawn squad try catch async await yield true false null`.
- `for i, x in array` does not work. Use `for e in enumerate(array) { e.index, e.value }`.
- No `|x| ...` closures and no arrow functions. Write `fn(x) { return ... }`.
- No `throw`, no `elif`, no `??` and no `? :` operator. Use `Err`/`?`, `else if`, `get(obj, key, default)` and `if c { a } else { b }`.
- Method chains cannot start a line with `.`; keep `a.filter(...).map(...)` on one line.
- `regex.*` takes `(text, pattern)`, not `(pattern, text)`. Escape backslashes in patterns: `"\\d+"`.
- `reduce(array, initial, fn)` — the initial value comes second.
- `push(xs, v)` returns a new array: write `xs = push(xs, v)` or `xs.push(v)`, never a bare `push(xs, v)` statement (edition 2027 rejects it, T0019). In 2027 `let ys = push(xs, v)` leaves `xs` unchanged (safe in backtracking); edition 2026 also updated a mutable `xs` there.
- Put non-String values into text with interpolation (`"total: {n}"`) or `str(n)`, never `"total: " + n`: edition 2027 rejects `+` between a String and a non-String (E0034; edition 2026 converts silently).
- No format specs such as `{x:.2f}` or `%.2f`: write `"{to_fixed(x, 2)}"`.
- Mutating a field or index requires a `let mut` binding.
- A method that changes its receiver must be declared `fn name(mut it, ...)` and called on a `let mut` variable (or a field/index of one); a plain `fn name(it)` cannot assign to `it`.
- `trim`/`upper`/`lower` are methods (`s.trim()`). `wait(n)` takes seconds; `await_timeout`/`select` take milliseconds. Statement forms take a unit after the number: `wait 250 ms`, `timeout 0.5 seconds { ... }`, `schedule every 2 minutes { ... }` (units `ms`/`millisecond(s)`, `second(s)`, `minute(s)`, `hour(s)`; fractions are exact; no unit means seconds); a `timeout` that expires raises E0031 `timeout: operation exceeded 0.5 second limit`.
- Shell builtins need `forge --allow-run run`. The HTTP client refuses private/loopback hosts unless `FORGE_HTTP_ALLOW_PRIVATE=1`.
- Always pass user input to SQL as a params array: `db.query("... WHERE id = ?", [id])`.

## Engine notes (v0.9.x)

The default bytecode VM and the reference interpreter run the full Forge test suite identically; `cargo test --test engine_diff` gates every example and fixture on both. Programs the VM compiler cannot handle fall back to the interpreter automatically; `@server` programs are served by the VM. Force the interpreter with `forge --interp run`.
